block.title: What is waiting on your machine?
block.body: On one machine you own, list the services waiting for traffic. First look at the local address: the same port can face only this machine, your LAN, or every interface. Record what you see before you change anything.

block.heading: A port has an entrance
block.alt: One owned machine shows a loopback-only service on 127.0.0.1:3000, a LAN-bound service on 192.168.1.23:8080, and a wildcard listener on 0.0.0.0:8443. Only the latter two may accept traffic from another device, depending on the network and firewall.
block.caption: Example IPv4 addresses. The arrows show possible bind scope, not proof that another device can connect.

block.heading: Read the address before the port
block.body: A process opens a socket at a local address and port. TCP LISTEN means it is waiting for a connection. UDP has sockets too, but no TCP-style LISTEN state. Think of a port as a door number and the bind address as which entrance that door faces. 127.0.0.1 and ::1 face only this machine. 0.0.0.0 and :: mean all available IPv4 or IPv6 interfaces, respectively. A specific LAN address faces that interface. None of these alone proves another device can get through the firewall.

block.heading: Three example lines, not your machine
block.code:
# Simplified synthetic output: protocol  local address:port  process
TCP  127.0.0.1:3000     preview-app
TCP  0.0.0.0:8443       web-server
UDP  192.168.1.23:5353  discovery-daemon

block.heading: Turn the lines into an inventory
rows: Local preview. Confirm the process if you did not start it.
May accept on any IPv4 interface; firewall may block it
What started the server? Check its configuration.
Bound to this LAN address; firewall may block traffic
Unknown until you check the process. UDP is not a TCP listener.
block.caption: These names and addresses are invented. Possible reach is not a connectivity test.

block.heading: Inspect one owned machine (read-only)
block.code:
# Linux: TCP listeners, then UDP sockets; -p asks for process names
sudo ss -ltnp
sudo ss -lunp

# macOS: TCP LISTEN sockets, then UDP sockets
sudo lsof -nP -iTCP -sTCP:LISTEN
sudo lsof -nP -iUDP

# Windows PowerShell: TCP listeners and UDP endpoints
Get-NetTCPConnection -State Listen | Select-Object LocalAddress,LocalPort,OwningProcess
Get-NetUDPEndpoint | Select-Object LocalAddress,LocalPort,OwningProcess
# For one PID you found in either list:
Get-Process -Id <PID> | Select-Object Id,ProcessName

block.heading: What the listing does and does not say
block.body: Run commands only on a machine you own or are authorized to inspect. sudo on Linux or macOS may ask for your password; an elevated PowerShell may show more process details. If process names are missing, record the PID or an unknown rather than guessing. A loopback bind is local to that host. A wildcard or LAN bind could be reachable from another device, but firewall rules, routing, and active interfaces still decide whether it is. Do not test another person’s device, stop an unfamiliar process, or change firewall rules based on this list. Look up the owning application first.

block.heading: Does the address change the answer?
block.prompt: On your own laptop, TCP port 9000 is bound to 127.0.0.1. Your LAN IP is 192.168.1.23. What does the listing alone tell you?
options: Any device on the Wi-Fi can connect because port 9000 is open
Only processes on this laptop can connect directly to that loopback socket
block.explanation: 127.0.0.1 is loopback on this machine. It does not face the LAN, regardless of the port number. A LAN-bound or wildcard socket would still require a separate firewall and routing check before calling it reachable.
